name: Prison Policy Initiative (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: incarcerated people and their families in the United States (federal phone caps, state free-call laws, decarceration).
summary: Prison Policy Initiative is a small US research and advocacy group on mass incarceration (1.9 million dollars spent in the year to June 2025). Its spending over fiscal years 2021-2025 is counted as a past average over the wins of those years: a share of the federal caps on prison and jail phone rates that the Martha Wright-Reed Act of 2022 made possible (still saving families about 200 million dollars a year after the FCC raised the caps in 2025), a smaller share of five states' free-call laws, and a very small share of the people kept out of prison by the reforms its data fed, each valued on the site's shared scales; all three branches are discounted for missing data. The result is about 0.04 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars, below the median of the site's global-health models: money saved by poor American families is worth little on a scale set by the world's poorest, and PPI holds about five years of spending in reserve, so the next dollar counts at a quarter of the average. The biggest uncertainties are PPI's share of the phone-rate campaign and how long the caps hold.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

rows.label: Consumption per person in families of incarcerated people (US$ a year)
rows.explainer: People in prison and their families are mostly poor: the shared US consumer expenditure per person times the lowest fifth's share, the same shared figures the site's US models use.

rows.label: Consumption per person of those who pay instead (US$ a year)
rows.explainer: Lower phone bills are paid for by the phone companies' owners, the prisons and jails that lose commissions, and (for free calls) state taxpayers: the average American, the shared figure.

rows.label: Value of a dollar families save, net of what the payers lose (units of value)
rows.explainer: On the site's log scale a small change in consumption is worth the dollars over consumption per person (spread over a household, household size cancels): the families' gain less the payers' loss, so a transfer counts only for going to poorer people.

rows.label: Yearly savings to families the FCC's 2024 caps would have brought

source.title: Worth Rises, FCC votes unanimously to significantly lower phone and video communication costs (18 July 2024)
source.quote: the new rules will save impacted families at least $500 million annually

rows.explainer: The FCC's July 2024 order under the Martha Wright-Reed Act (2022), which for the first time covered calls within a state: advocates put the savings at at least $500 million a year, the FCC's draft at $386 million. Our estimate 450 million, from 386 to 550 million.

rows.label: Yearly savings lost when the FCC raised the caps in October 2025

source.title: Worth Rises, Worth Rises condemns FCC rollback of correctional telecom regulations (29 October 2025)
source.quote: will deliver substantially less financial relief to families impacted by incarceration — at least $215 million less per year

rows.explainer: The interim caps of October 2025 (11 cents a minute at most prisons, 10 to 19 cents at jails, in effect from 5 December 2025 and to be met by 6 April 2026, Prison Legal News, February 2026) are higher than the 2024 caps but still cap in-state jail calls that had cost up to 76 cents a minute. At least 215 million a year less relief; our estimate 250 million, from 215 to 320 million.

rows.explainer: What the federal win still saves families each year: mostly in jails, since 94% of prisons already charge less than the new caps (Prison Legal News).

rows.label: Years from the federal win until it takes effect
rows.explainer: The Act passed in January 2023; caps that bind took effect in December 2025 and must be met by April 2026: about 3 years, from 2 to 4.

Fewer people incarcerated through the reforms of 2020-2025 PPI's research and support fed
rows.explainer: PPI supplies the data behind bail, sentencing, parole and jail-expansion fights and gave technical support to advocates in 24 states (audit note 1). The country held nearly 2 million people in 2025, about 13% below the pre-pandemic level (The Whole Pie 2025), much of the fall from the pandemic itself and some refilled since. Our judgment: the reforms won in the period keep 50,000 people out, from 10,000 to 150,000.

rows.label: Wins not modelled one by one, as a share of the modelled wins
rows.explainer: PPI's campaign against prison gerrymandering (states counting incarcerated people at home for redistricting, a change in more than a dozen states, several in the period), its work against medical copays, release-card and other fees, bans on replacing in-person visits with paid video calls, and local fights against jail expansion. Each is smaller per person than the phone and decarceration wins or hard to value (representation): together 30% of the modelled value, from 0 to 100%.

rows.label: Side effect: more contact with family, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Cheaper calls mean more of them; contact with family in prison is linked to less depression and to fewer returns to prison (studies of visits; a 2026 report linking free calls to better re-entry). Not in the money valued above: 10%, from 0 to 40%.

rows.label: Side effect: providers cutting service under lower caps, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Providers and jails argued that lower caps would cut phones, hours or security screening; little evidence of it so far: -3%, from -10% to 0.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: The sum of the two side effects above.
